chunks: What non-volatile memory means. The question: What does non-volatile (NV) memory mean?
Non-volatile memory keeps its contents when the power is off. Volatile memory, such as SRAM, forgets at once.
Flash and EEPROM store each bit as a tiny amount of electric charge trapped on an insulated island inside a transistor.
The price is that changing the bit is slower and wears the memory a little each time.
Picture marbles in a sealed jar. With the lid on, they stay put for years, so no power is needed. To change them you must open the lid with a strong push, which is slow.
Each opening scuffs the lid, so it can be done only so many times. Volatile memory is more like a spinning plate on a stick. It stays up only while you keep it moving.
The two stored states are just a low- V t and a high- V t transistor. The read circuit applies a gate voltage between the two thresholds and senses whether current flows.
Volatile: loses its data when power is removed. Non-volatile: keeps its data without power.
Floating gate: a tiny electrically isolated island inside a transistor that traps charge. Endurance: how many write and erase cycles a cell survives.
Retention: how long data stays valid with no power, typically 10 to 20 years.
To write a bit in flash, a high voltage pushes electrons through a thin insulating layer onto the floating gate. The trapped charge changes how easily the transistor turns on.
To read, the chip checks whether it turns on at a test voltage. With the power off, the electrons stay trapped.
A cell rated for 100,000 cycles that is rewritten once a day lasts about 274 years. Rewritten once a second, it lasts about 28 hours. That is the whole idea.
"Non-volatile memory retains its data without power, unlike SRAM or DRAM.
Flash and EEPROM do it by trapping charge on an insulated floating gate, which shifts the transistor's threshold voltage; FRAM and MRAM use ferroelectric or magnetic states.
The trade-off is slower, more power-hungry writes and limited endurance, so firmware lives in flash while running variables live in SRAM."
